o: We must decide whether a 3x3 board is reachable in a legal game where X moves first and players alternate. Reachability is fully determined by counts and win states: X's count must equal O's count or exceed it by exactly one, a game cannot continue after someone wins, and both players cannot have winning lines simultaneously. Example 1 fails because O appears with zero X's. Example 2 has 3 X's and 1 O — an impossible count difference. Example 3 has 5 X's and 4 O's, no winner, so it is valid. The tiny fixed board (3x3) means even exhaustive search over all games is feasible, but a direct condition check is cleaner.
k: X count minus O count must be exactly 0 or 1; anything else is unreachable.
If X wins, the board must show one more X than O; if O wins, counts must be equal.
X and O can never both have winning lines at once (they would require different move counts).
The board is only 9 cells, so brute-force enumeration of all games is also viable.

a.i: Replay every possible game from the empty board via DFS: at each turn try placing the current player's mark in every empty cell. If we ever reach the target board, it is valid. Prune by stopping recursion when the game is over (a winner exists or board full). With at most 9! move orderings and early termination on wins, this easily fits limits.
s: Convert the target board to a tuple for comparison.
DFS(state, turn): if state equals target, return true.
If state has a winner or is full, return false.
For each empty cell, place turn's mark and recurse with flipped turn.
Return whether any branch reached the target.
a.t: O(9!) worst case — DFS explores permutations of up to 9 moves with pruning on finished games.
a.sp: O(9) recursion depth plus visited-state storage.

a.i: Reachability reduces to arithmetic on counts and winners. Since X starts, cx - co must be 0 or 1. If X has won, the last move was X's, so cx = co + 1; if O has won, the last move was O's, so cx = co. Both cannot win simultaneously since that would demand contradictory counts. If these checks pass, a valid move sequence always exists (fill cells in any order consistent with the counts, stopping at the win).
s: Count X's and O's; reject unless diff = cx - co is 0 or 1.
Write a helper that detects whether a player has any complete row, column, or diagonal.
If X wins, require diff == 1; otherwise reject.
If O wins, require diff == 0; otherwise reject.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def validTicTacToe(self, board):
        cx = sum(r.count('X') for r in board)
        co = sum(r.count('O') for r in board)
        if not (0 <= cx - co <= 1): return False
        def wins(p):
            for i in range(3):
                if all(board[i][j] == p for j in range(3)): return True
                if all(board[j][i] == p for j in range(3)): return True
            if all(board[i][i] == p for i in range(3)): return True
            if all(board[i][2-i] == p for i in range(3)): return True
            return False
        wx, wo = wins('X'), wins('O')
        if wx and cx != co + 1: return False
        if wo and cx != co: return False
        if wx and wo: return False
        return True

a.t: O(1) — constant work over a fixed 3x3 grid (at most a few dozen comparisons).

w: In an interview, lead with the counting approach after briefly noting brute force exists; it demonstrates the key insight that turn order forces exact count relationships. Common pitfalls: forgetting that a winner fixes the exact count difference (not just a bound), missing the impossibility of double winners, and allowing negative count differences. Edge cases to test: empty board (valid), full draw boards, boards where the loser also completed a line after the game should have ended, and boards with extra moves past a win. Follow-ups might generalize to n x n boards with k-in-a-row, or ask you to reconstruct a valid move sequence — the same counting logic extends naturally.
